seo.description: Compare GIA, IGI and HRD diamond reports and learn how lab recognition, report type, verification and grading consistency can affect an offer.

title: How to Read and Verify a Diamond Grading Report Before Selling
excerpt: A diamond report can help you understand and sell your stone, but only when it is authentic and matches the physical diamond. Learn how to check the report number, 4Cs, measurements, clarity plot, comments, treatments and laser inscription.
content_html:
A diamond grading report contains much more than the four headline grades. It can identify whether the stone is natural or laboratory-grown, record its measurements and document characteristics that affect its appearance, marketability and resale value.

Before selling, you should verify that the report exists in the issuing laboratory’s official database. You must then establish that the physical diamond is the same stone described in that record.

These are separate checks. A genuine report number proves that a laboratory record exists. It does not prove that the ring or loose stone in front of you matches that report.

Shape, measurements, carat weight, clarity characteristics and any laser inscription can help connect the document with the diamond. Physical inspection is also needed to confirm that the stone has not been chipped, repolished, recut or treated since grading.

Quick Answer: How Do You Check a Diamond Certificate?

Find the issuing laboratory and unique report number on the document. Enter that number directly into the laboratory’s official report-verification website and compare the returned information with the paper or digital report.

Check the diamond’s natural or laboratory-grown description, shape, carat weight, measurements, colour, clarity, cut information and grading date. Any discrepancy should be investigated.

The physical diamond must then be matched to the record. A professional can inspect the laser inscription, measurements and clarity characteristics.

Do not rely only on a QR code, screenshot or report number. An authentic report can still be presented with the wrong diamond.

Diamond Certificate vs Diamond Grading Report

People commonly ask how to read a diamond certificate, but “grading report” is usually the more accurate term.

A grading report records findings from a laboratory examination. Depending on the service, it may describe the diamond’s origin, weight, quality characteristics, measurements, finish, fluorescence and known treatments.

It is not generally a guarantee of future value. It does not require a buyer to pay a specific amount, and it does not prove ownership.

An insurance appraisal, purchase invoice or jeweller’s valuation serves a different purpose. Those documents may contain a monetary figure, but they do not necessarily provide an independent laboratory grade.

Begin by Identifying the Issuing Laboratory

The report should clearly state which organisation examined the diamond. GIA, IGI and HRD Antwerp are examples of laboratories whose reports are commonly encountered in international diamond markets.

Check the exact name and official domain rather than trusting a similar-looking logo. Fraudulent documents can imitate laboratory branding.

Use the laboratory’s official website to access its report-check service. Type the address yourself or reach it through a trusted search result instead of depending exclusively on a QR code printed on an unfamiliar document.

Different laboratories use different terminology and formats. Read the scale and explanations printed on the report rather than assuming that every abbreviation has the same meaning.

Our separate guide compares GIA, IGI and HRD diamond reports.

Identify the Exact Report Type

A laboratory may offer several document types. A full natural-diamond grading report, dossier, digital report, jewellery report, coloured-diamond report and laboratory-grown assessment do not necessarily contain the same information.

Some reports contain a detailed clarity plot. Compact formats may not. Some services include a laser inscription, while others make it optional.

A loose-diamond report can normally provide more precise weight and measurements because the entire stone is accessible. A jewellery report may describe a mounted item within the physical limitations created by its setting.

Understanding the report type prevents you from treating an omitted field as evidence that the document is incomplete or false.

How to Read the Main Fields on a Diamond Report

Although layouts differ, these are the principal fields likely to affect identification and resale assessment.

The report must be interpreted as one connected description. No single field establishes authenticity or value by itself.

How to Use the Diamond Report Number

The diamond report number is the starting point for verification.

Enter it exactly as printed, including any leading zeros, letters or separators required by the laboratory. A typing error can produce a false “not found” result.

The online record should display information corresponding with the report. Compare the carat weight, shape, colour, clarity, measurements and date instead of stopping when the number produces a result.

A report number is not a serial number proving ownership. It identifies a laboratory record associated with an examined item.

How to Verify a GIA Report

Open GIA’s official Report Check service and enter the report number.

Compare the online result with every major field on the document. The report type, issue date, shape, measurements, carat weight, colour, clarity and cut-related information should correspond.

Some GIA services provide a downloadable digital report or additional images. Available features depend on the report type and date.

If the record differs from the document, stop and investigate. Do not assume that a paper containing a valid GIA number is authentic simply because the number exists.

How to Verify an IGI Report

Use IGI’s official report-verification page and enter the unique report number. Some reports may also contain a QR code, but the official database should remain the reference point.

Compare the returned record with the report’s description, shape, measurements and 4Cs information.

Confirm whether the report describes a natural diamond, laboratory-grown diamond or complete jewellery item. Those categories must not be treated as interchangeable.

Where a laser inscription is stated, it can support physical matching under magnification.

How to Verify an HRD Antwerp Report

Use HRD Antwerp’s official report-check service and enter the report number shown on the document.

Review the returned report data and compare it with the physical document. Pay attention to the colour and clarity scales because HRD terminology can differ from that used on another laboratory’s report.

Confirm whether the report covers a natural diamond, laboratory-grown diamond, coloured diamond or jewellery item.

If the record cannot be located, check the number carefully and contact the laboratory or a qualified professional before concluding that the document is false.

Why Online Verification Is Not Enough

Online verification confirms that a laboratory has a record under that number. It does not prove that the stone being offered is the diamond described.

A genuine report can be copied. Its number can also be inscribed fraudulently onto another stone or placed on an imitation document.

The buyer should match the physical diamond using several characteristics. Shape, measurements, weight, clarity features and inscription provide stronger evidence when considered together.

For a valuable diamond, specialist origin and treatment testing may also be required. Visual inspection alone cannot always distinguish a natural diamond from a laboratory-grown diamond or detect sophisticated treatments.

How to Read the Report Date

The report date shows when the laboratory examined the diamond. It is not an expiry date.

A diamond’s inherent carat, colour and clarity characteristics are generally stable, but its physical condition can change. The stone may be chipped, abraded, repolished or recut after grading.

Treatments may also have been applied after the original examination. A setting can be changed, and the report may become separated from the item it originally described.

An older report can still be useful when it is authentic and matches an unchanged stone. Physical inspection determines whether its description remains accurate.

Natural vs Laboratory-Grown Description

One of the most important report fields is the description of the diamond’s growth origin.

The document should indicate whether the laboratory identified the stone as natural or laboratory-grown. Never infer origin from appearance, price or a seller’s verbal statement.

A laboratory-grown diamond is a real diamond, but it participates in a different resale market from a natural diamond.

“Natural” in this context does not necessarily identify the country or mine where the diamond originated. Geographic origin requires specific evidence and, in some cases, a dedicated origin-report service.

How to Read Shape and Cutting Style

Shape describes the diamond’s face-up outline, such as round, oval, cushion, emerald, pear, radiant or marquise.

Cutting style describes the arrangement of facets. A report might use descriptions such as round brilliant, oval brilliant or emerald cut.

The physical diamond should clearly correspond with this field. A report for a round brilliant cannot belong to an oval stone even if the carat, colour and clarity appear similar.

For unusual or antique cuts, the description may differ from everyday jewellery terminology. A professional can explain how the laboratory classified the stone.

How to Read Diamond Measurements

Diamond measurements are recorded in millimetres.

A round diamond is normally described using its minimum diameter, maximum diameter and depth. Fancy shapes are generally recorded through length, width and depth.

Measurements help distinguish one stone from another and reveal how the carat weight is distributed. Two one-carat diamonds can have different face-up dimensions.

A mounted diamond can be measured approximately, but the setting may obstruct the girdle or pavilion. Small tolerances are possible, so professional interpretation is important.

A substantial measurement mismatch is a warning sign that the report may not belong to the stone.

How to Read Carat Weight

Carat is a measure of weight. One metric carat equals 0.20 grams.

Laboratories weigh loose diamonds using precise equipment. A report might record 0.99, 1.00, 1.01 or another exact weight.

A mounted diamond cannot normally be weighed separately without professional removal. An appraiser may estimate its weight from measurements, but that estimate is not equivalent to a laboratory weighing.

Do not remove a diamond merely to confirm carat weight before obtaining professional advice. The setting may have independent brand, antique or craftsmanship value.

How to Read Diamond Colour Grade

For natural diamonds in the standard colour range, D represents colourless, with increasing traces of yellow, brown or grey towards Z.

Each letter represents a narrow range rather than an exact point. The report’s laboratory and scale must be considered when interpreting the grade.

Fancy-colour diamonds use a separate system involving colour hue, intensity and distribution. A Z-colour diamond should not automatically be described as Fancy Yellow.

The report comments should be checked for colour treatment. A treated diamond should not be compared directly with a naturally coloured diamond based only on appearance.

Read our guide to how colour grade affects diamond resale value.

How to Read Diamond Clarity Grade

Clarity evaluates the relative absence of internal inclusions and surface blemishes.

The GIA scale ranges from Flawless through Internally Flawless, VVS, VS and SI to Included grades. Other laboratories may use different abbreviations, so consult the scale on the report.

Clarity is assessed under controlled conditions and magnification. An SI diamond may appear clean without magnification, while another stone with the same grade may contain a more visible inclusion.

The plot and report comments can explain why the grade was assigned. The physical inclusion appearance and current condition still require examination.

Our detailed guide explains how clarity and inclusions affect diamond resale value.

How to Read the Clarity Plot

A clarity plotting diagram maps important internal and external characteristics.

On many GIA plots, red symbols indicate internal characteristics, while green symbols represent external features. Always use the legend printed on the report because colours and symbols can vary by laboratory.

The plot can help identify the diamond because no two stones are expected to have the same pattern of characteristics in precisely the same positions.

A plot is not always a complete microscopic map. Some characteristics may be described in comments, and some compact report types may omit the plot entirely.

Professional matching requires the plotted features to be located in the physical diamond under magnification.

How to Read the Cut Grade

Cut grade evaluates aspects of a diamond’s proportions, light performance and workmanship where an applicable grading system exists.

On a standard GIA report, an overall cut grade applies to qualifying round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z range. Fancy shapes do not receive that same overall GIA cut grade.

Do not assume that an oval or emerald diamond is poorly cut because the field is absent. Its proportions, polish, symmetry, outline and appearance must be evaluated differently.

Similarly, the word “Excellent” should be interpreted within the issuing laboratory’s system rather than treated as a universal guarantee.

Read more about how cut grade affects diamond resale value.

How to Read Polish and Symmetry

Polish describes the quality and condition of the facet surfaces. Symmetry describes the precision of the outline and facet arrangement.

These grades commonly range from Excellent to Poor, although terminology can vary.

A diamond with Excellent cut may have Very Good polish or symmetry. Triple Excellent means that the overall cut, polish and symmetry grades are all Excellent on an applicable round-brilliant report.

Current condition matters. Abrasion or later repolishing may mean an old report no longer fully describes the stone.

How to Read Fluorescence

Fluorescence describes the diamond’s reaction to long-wave ultraviolet light.

Common intensity descriptions include None, Faint, Medium, Strong and Very Strong. Blue is the most frequently encountered fluorescence colour.

Fluorescence does not change the laboratory colour grade. Its effect on appearance and market demand can be positive, negative or neutral depending on the diamond.

Strong fluorescence does not automatically mean the stone is hazy. Transparency must be examined physically.

Our guide to fluorescence, polish and symmetry resale value explains these characteristics further.

How to Read the Proportions Diagram

A proportions diagram shows information about the diamond’s physical design.

Depending on shape and report type, it may include table percentage, total depth, crown angle, pavilion angle, girdle thickness and culet information.

These numbers help a buyer understand weight distribution and potential appearance. They should not be interpreted independently.

There is no single measurement that proves a diamond is beautifully cut. The angles, percentages, finish and physical appearance work together.

Why the Girdle Description Matters

The girdle forms the outer edge between the crown and pavilion.

A very thin area may be more vulnerable to damage, while a very thick girdle can retain weight without increasing face-up size. Girdle thickness can also vary around the stone.

The laser inscription, when present, is generally placed on the girdle. A setting may conceal it.

The girdle description contributes to cut and durability assessment but does not determine value alone.

How to Read Culet Information

The culet is the small facet or point at the bottom of the pavilion.

Many modern diamonds have no culet or a very small one. Larger culets can be intentional in antique diamonds and may be visible face-up.

A large culet does not automatically indicate damage. In an old European or old mine diamond, it may be part of the historical cutting style.

The buyer should interpret it according to the diamond’s age, shape and market.

Why Report Comments Are Important

Report comments can disclose information not fully represented in the headline grades or plotting diagram.

They may refer to laser inscriptions, treatments, internal graining, clouds, clarity characteristics not shown, additional facets or other identifying observations.

A comment can materially affect resale interpretation. Never submit only a cropped image of the 4Cs.

Upload every page and keep the comments legible. A buyer should explain any value adjustment based on a report comment.

How Treatments Appear on a Report

Appropriate laboratory reports may disclose detected colour or clarity treatments according to the laboratory’s policies.

Examples include laser drilling, HPHT processing, irradiation or other treatment. Fracture-filled and coated diamonds may require different report services or identification documents.

Treatment information can appear in the description, results or comments. It should never be hidden when requesting an offer.

A natural diamond with treated colour is not equivalent to an untreated natural diamond of similar visible colour.

How to Check a Laser Inscription

A laser inscription is microscopic wording or a number placed on the diamond’s girdle.

It is not normally visible without magnification. A professional can rotate the diamond under a loupe or microscope to locate and read it.

Compare the inscription exactly with the report and official online record. The measurements and other identifying characteristics should also match.

A missing inscription does not automatically invalidate a report because not every report service includes one. A setting can also hide part of the girdle.

Why an Inscription Alone Cannot Prove Identity

A report number can be copied or fraudulently inscribed.

The inscription must therefore be supported by the correct shape, measurements, quality characteristics and, where available, clarity plot.

Professional verification may also include testing the material and confirming whether it is natural or laboratory-grown.

Treat the inscription as one useful identifier—not as complete proof.

Paper Reports vs Digital Reports

Some laboratories issue paper reports, while others provide digital-only documents for certain services.

A digital report is not automatically less legitimate. Its authenticity depends on whether it is available through the issuing laboratory’s official system and matches the diamond.

A paper report is not automatically genuine. Printing quality, logos and security features can be imitated.

The official database and physical diamond match are more important than whether the document is printed.

Security Features on a Paper Report

Laboratory reports may include holograms, microprinting, security screens, specialised paper or other anti-counterfeit features.

These features vary by laboratory, report type and issue date. Do not reject an older document because it lacks a feature used on newer reports.

Security features can support authenticity, but they should not replace online verification.

If the document appears altered, has inconsistent fonts or contains information that differs from the online record, request professional review.

What If the Report Number Cannot Be Found?

First, re-enter the number carefully. Check for leading zeros, letters, spaces or confusion between similar characters.

Confirm that you are using the correct laboratory’s official verification service. A number from an appraisal or retailer is not necessarily a laboratory report number.

Older reports or unusual services may require direct contact with the issuing laboratory.

Until the document is verified, treat its grades as unconfirmed. Do not advertise the diamond using unsupported laboratory claims.

What If the Online Record Differs From the Paper?

Stop the transaction until the discrepancy is explained.

A minor formatting difference may result from an updated digital presentation, but the identifying and grading data should correspond.

Differences in carat, shape, measurements, colour or clarity are significant. The paper could be altered, paired with the wrong report number or associated with another diamond.

Contact the laboratory or obtain independent professional inspection before proceeding.

How to Match Measurements With a Mounted Diamond

A professional can often estimate or partially measure a mounted diamond, but metal may obstruct some dimensions.

The reported shape and visible measurements should still be broadly consistent. A large mismatch is not explained simply by the setting.

Exact weight cannot normally be confirmed while the diamond remains mounted. If removal becomes necessary, it should be performed professionally after evaluating the setting.

Do not damage a branded or antique ring merely to conduct a check that may be completed through other identifying characteristics.

How to Match a Clarity Plot With the Diamond

A gemologist uses magnification to locate the inclusions and blemishes represented on the report.

The position, type and relationship of these characteristics can create an identifying pattern. A central crystal, feather near the girdle or group of pinpoints may support the match.

The process requires skill because facet reflections can make one inclusion appear multiple times.

A plot mismatch can indicate the wrong diamond, later recutting or an incomplete interpretation. It should be investigated rather than ignored.

Does the Report Still Apply After Recutting?

Usually not in its original form.

Recutting can change carat weight, measurements, shape, cut, polish, symmetry and clarity. The laser inscription may also be removed.

Even limited repolishing can alter dimensions or surface characteristics.

A diamond that has undergone material alteration may require an updated report before the old grades are used in a sale.

Does the Report Still Apply After Damage?

It can remain useful for identification, but it may not describe current quality accurately.

A new chip can affect clarity, weight and durability. Abrasion may change polish or condition.

The buyer should distinguish between an authentic historical report and the stone’s present state.

Any offer adjustment should be based on the actual damage and likely repair consequences.

Grading Report vs Insurance Appraisal

A grading report describes gemological characteristics. An insurance appraisal generally estimates replacement value.

The appraisal figure may be substantially different from the amount available through resale. It can also include the setting, taxes, retail margins and replacement considerations.

A grading laboratory does not normally state what a buyer must pay.

When selling, the relevant figure is the current market offer for the verified diamond or jewellery—not the insurance replacement amount.

Grading Report vs Purchase Receipt

A receipt shows what someone paid at a particular time and may help establish provenance.

It does not prove current value, condition or grading accuracy. The retail price may include taxes, design, brand, store costs and services.

The grading report provides more useful quality information, but it also does not establish resale value alone.

Submit both documents when available, but understand their different purposes.

Does a Grading Report Prove Ownership?

No. A report follows the diamond’s identifying characteristics, not the identity of its legal owner.

A seller may still need identification, proof of ownership, inheritance information or other transaction documents.

A report number should never be treated as authority to sell an item.

Read our guide to documents needed to sell a diamond.

Does a Verified Report State the Diamond’s Resale Value?

No. Verification confirms the report record and helps identify the diamond.

The buyer must still calculate value using the verified grades, physical condition, origin and current demand.

Two diamonds with the same grades can receive different offers because of inclusion appearance, proportions, shape, fluorescence or condition.

Our pillar guide explains how diamond buyers calculate an offer.

Illustrative Example: Valid Number, Wrong Measurements

Imagine a fictional report for a 1.01-carat round diamond measuring approximately 6.4 millimetres across.

The online record is genuine, but the diamond presented with it measures significantly less and has different proportions.

The valid report number does not resolve the mismatch. The buyer should stop and determine whether the wrong stone or document has been supplied.

Illustrative Example: Correct Report, Later Chip

Consider a fictional oval diamond with a genuine, verifiable report.

The measurements and inscription match, but physical inspection reveals a chip near one end that is not documented on the older report.

The report still helps identify the diamond, but the final offer must account for current condition, possible repair and weight-loss risk.

Illustrative Example: A Hidden Inscription

Imagine a diamond ring whose verified report states that the girdle carries a laser inscription.

The inscription cannot be seen because a prong covers that part of the girdle. This does not automatically prove a mismatch.

A professional may use measurements and clarity characteristics first. Removal should only be considered if required for the final verification.

Illustrative Example: Natural vs Laboratory-Grown Confusion

Suppose a seller uploads a report and describes the diamond as natural.

The document’s description actually states that the stone is laboratory-grown. The carat, colour and clarity fields cannot be used to value it as a natural diamond.

The origin field must be read before any price comparison is made.

Illustrative Example: A Missing Clarity Plot

A compact report contains colour, clarity, carat and measurements but no plotting diagram.

The absence of a plot does not automatically make the report invalid. The selected service may not include one.

The buyer can use the report number, inscription, measurements and physical examination to establish whether the diamond matches.

Preparing a Report for an Online Valuation

Scan or photograph the complete report in clear, neutral light. Include every page, comment, scale, barcode and report number.

Do not obscure the characteristics required for verification. You can remove unrelated personal information from invoices or appraisals before uploading them.

Photograph the diamond or complete jewellery item from the front, side and underside. Include the inside of the band if it contains hallmarks, serial numbers or signatures.

An online review can establish useful preliminary information. A final offer may still require physical verification.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I check whether a diamond certificate is real?

Verify the report number through the issuing laboratory’s official website and compare the record with both the document and physical diamond.

Where is the diamond report number?

It is normally printed prominently near the top of the report. Its position depends on the laboratory and document format.

Is the report number the same as a serial number?

It identifies the laboratory record. It does not prove ownership or automatically identify the jewellery setting.

Can I verify a GIA report for free?

GIA provides an official online Report Check service for report verification.

Can I verify an IGI report online?

Yes. IGI provides an official report-verification service.

Can I verify an HRD report online?

Yes. HRD Antwerp provides an official report-check service for supported reports.

Does a valid report number prove my diamond is genuine?

No. It proves the record exists. The physical diamond must still match it.

Can a fake diamond have a genuine report number?

A valid number could be copied or fraudulently inscribed onto another material or stone. Professional matching is essential.

Can someone copy a diamond certificate?

A document or number can be copied. That is why database and physical verification are both required.

Should I trust a report QR code?

Use it cautiously and confirm that it leads to the laboratory’s official domain. You can also type the official address manually.

Is a screenshot of a report enough?

No. Verify the number independently and request the complete document.

Is a digital diamond report genuine?

It can be. Some laboratory services are digital-only. Verify it through the official database.

Is a paper certificate automatically genuine?

No. Paper documents can be altered or counterfeited.

What information should match the online report?

The report type, date, shape, measurements, carat, colour, clarity and other grading fields should correspond.

What if one field does not match?

Stop and investigate. A material discrepancy may indicate an altered document or mismatched diamond.

Can two diamonds have the same carat, colour and clarity?

Yes. Those grades alone cannot prove identity.

Can two diamonds have identical measurements?

They can have similar measurements. Clarity characteristics and inscriptions provide additional identification.

Is a laser inscription visible without magnification?

Usually not. It is normally read using a loupe or microscope.

Where is the laser inscription?

It is generally placed on the diamond’s girdle.

Does every certified diamond have a laser inscription?

No. Availability depends on the laboratory, report type and selected service.

Can a setting hide the inscription?

Yes. A prong or bezel may cover part of the girdle.

Can a laser inscription be removed?

Repolishing or recutting can remove or alter an inscription.

Does an inscription guarantee the diamond’s value?

No. It helps with identification but does not state monetary value.

Can a report be verified without an inscription?

Yes. Measurements, weight, shape and clarity characteristics can also support matching.

What does the report date mean?

It is the date the laboratory examined the diamond. It is not necessarily an expiry date.

Do diamond grading reports expire?

They do not usually have a simple expiry date, but condition or report relevance can change.

Is a twenty-year-old GIA report still useful?

Potentially. It should be verified and the diamond’s current condition should be inspected.

Should I update an old report before selling?

Not automatically. Obtain an initial assessment and compare the expected benefit with the fee, time and risk.

What does “natural diamond” mean on the report?

It means the laboratory identified the examined stone as naturally formed rather than laboratory-grown.

Does natural origin identify the mine?

No. Geographic origin requires separate evidence or a specialised origin-report service.

How can I tell whether the report is for a lab-grown diamond?

Read the description and report title. Do not infer origin from the 4Cs alone.

Can natural and lab-grown reports look different?

Yes. Laboratories may use distinct formats or terminology to differentiate them.

What does carat mean?

Carat measures weight. One carat equals 0.20 grams.

Can I confirm exact carat weight while the diamond is mounted?

Normally not without professional removal. Measurements can only support an estimate.

What do the three diamond measurements mean?

For a fancy shape, they generally represent length, width and depth. A round normally uses minimum diameter, maximum diameter and depth.

Why do two one-carat diamonds have different measurements?

Carat measures weight, and that weight can be distributed differently through the diamond.

What does D colour mean?

D is the highest colourless grade on the standard D-to-Z scale.

Is Z a fancy-yellow diamond?

No. Z remains within the D-to-Z range. Fancy colour uses a separate grading system.

What does VS2 clarity mean?

It indicates minor inclusions within the relevant grading system. Actual inclusion type and position still matter.

What is a clarity plot?

It is a diagram mapping important inclusions and blemishes.

Does every report include a clarity plot?

No. Some compact or digital report types may omit it.

Does the clarity plot show every inclusion?

Not necessarily. Some characteristics may be described in comments or omitted from the simplified plot.

What do red and green marks mean on a GIA plot?

Red commonly represents internal characteristics and green represents external features. Always check the printed legend.

Can a clarity plot identify a diamond?

It can support identification when its characteristics are matched under magnification.

What does Excellent cut mean?

It is the highest grade within an applicable cut-grading system. It does not guarantee a particular resale value.

Why does my oval report have no cut grade?

Standard GIA reports do not assign the same overall cut grade to fancy shapes such as oval.

What are polish and symmetry?

Polish assesses facet-surface quality, while symmetry assesses outline and facet alignment.

What is Triple Excellent?

It describes a qualifying round brilliant with Excellent cut, polish and symmetry.

What does None fluorescence mean?

It means the reaction falls within the laboratory’s None category under its standard testing conditions.

Is Strong fluorescence bad?

Not automatically. Transparency, body colour and actual appearance must be evaluated.

What is the proportions diagram?

It records measurements and relationships such as table, depth, crown, pavilion, girdle and culet where applicable.

What does a thick girdle mean?

It indicates greater thickness around the diamond’s outer edge. Its effect depends on the complete proportions.

What does “culet: none” mean?

It means there is no additional flat facet of reportable size at the pavilion’s bottom.

Why are report comments important?

They can disclose treatments, inscriptions, graining or characteristics not fully shown elsewhere.

Where are treatments listed?

They may appear in the description, grading results or comments, depending on the laboratory and report.

Can a treated diamond still have a report?

Some treated diamonds can receive an appropriate report, while others may receive an identification document rather than a standard grading report.

Does a certificate show the diamond’s price?

A grading report normally does not state current resale value.

Is the price on my appraisal the resale value?

Usually not. Insurance appraisals generally estimate replacement cost.

Does a purchase receipt prove current value?

No. It shows a historical transaction, not present market value.

Does a grading report prove I own the diamond?

No. Ownership and authority to sell require separate evidence.

What if the paper report is lost?

The online record may still be available. A buyer can also assess a diamond without the original report.

Can I sell a diamond without a certificate?

Yes. Additional physical testing and grading may be needed before a final offer is confirmed.

Should I pay for a replacement report?

Only when the expected improvement in the sale outcome justifies the expense and risk.

Can a buyer reduce the offer if the report does not match?

Yes. A mismatch creates uncertainty and may require additional testing. The buyer should explain the issue.

Can damage make the report inaccurate?

Yes. A later chip, abrasion or recut can change the diamond’s documented condition or grades.

Should I remove the diamond to check the report?

Not yourself. Professional removal should only be considered when necessary.

Can a mounted diamond still be verified?

Often, yes. The report number, visible measurements, inscription and clarity features may provide sufficient initial evidence.

How should I upload my report for a valuation?

Upload every page clearly and include the report number, comments, measurements and scales.

Should I crop the report number from my submission?

No. A professional buyer needs it for verification. Remove only unrelated personal information from other documents.

Can Sothis verify my diamond report?

Sothis can review your report, check available laboratory records and compare the documented information with the diamond during physical verification.

Verify Your Report and Request a Market-Based Offer

A grading report is useful only when it is authentic, complete and correctly matched to the physical diamond.

Begin by submitting the full report and clear photographs of the diamond or jewellery. Sothis Diamonds can review the report number, origin, grades, measurements, comments and available identifying information.

If the original document is missing or cannot be verified, you can still request an assessment using the information available. Following physical inspection, you can receive a market-based offer that you remain free to accept or decline.

Request a free, no-obligation diamond valuation

title: How Accurate Are Online Diamond Value Calculators?
excerpt: Online diamond value calculators can provide a useful starting range when supplied with verified information. Discover what these tools calculate, which factors they miss and why physical inspection is normally required before confirming a resale offer.
content_html:
An online diamond value calculator can produce an estimate within seconds. Enter the carat weight, shape, colour, clarity and cut, and the tool may return what appears to be a precise monetary value.

That number should be treated as a starting point—not a guaranteed selling price.

Calculator accuracy depends on the information entered, the market data behind the tool and what type of value it is attempting to estimate. A calculator based on verified grading-report data may produce a useful range for a standard loose diamond. A tool using guessed grades, outdated prices or retail listings can produce a seriously misleading result.

Automated calculators also struggle with factors that require physical judgement. These include visible inclusions, transparency, damage, treatments, fancy-shape proportions, antique character and the value of a complete branded or period piece.

The most reliable process uses a calculator for orientation, an expert review for context and physical verification before a final offer.

Quick Answer: Are Diamond Value Calculators Accurate?

Online diamond value calculators can be reasonably useful for establishing a broad preliminary range when the diamond has a current, verifiable grading report and the calculator uses relevant market data.

They are less dependable when the origin, carat, colour, clarity or condition is unknown. A photograph cannot reliably establish all these characteristics, and a mounted diamond cannot normally be weighed precisely.

A calculator also needs to define what it is estimating. Retail price, insurance replacement value, private-sale asking price and immediate buyer offer are different figures.

No calculator can guarantee what you will receive. A final resale offer normally requires confirmation that the physical diamond matches the submitted information and remains in the documented condition.

What Does an Online Diamond Value Calculator Do?

A diamond calculator applies supplied characteristics to an underlying pricing model.

A basic model may use only carat, colour and clarity. More detailed calculators may also consider shape, cut, grading laboratory, polish, symmetry, fluorescence and natural or laboratory-grown origin.

The model then compares that combination with pricing data, previous transactions, current inventory or the buyer’s own purchasing criteria.

The apparent precision of the result does not prove accuracy. A calculator displaying €4,237 may still be less reliable than a specialist providing a well-supported range of €3,800 to €4,400.

Four Different Types of Online Diamond Valuation

Not every online tool performs the same task.

A calculator and a final purchase offer answer different questions and should not be presented as interchangeable.

Calculator Value vs Retail Price

Some calculators estimate the current price of a comparable new diamond sold through a retailer.

Retail pricing can include inventory costs, store overhead, marketing, warranties, sales services and profit margin. Taxes may also be included or excluded depending on the country and tool.

A buyer purchasing a pre-owned diamond does not usually pay the full retail replacement price. The buyer must verify, hold and resell the stone while assuming transaction risk.

A calculator based on retail listings can therefore be accurate for one purpose while being unsuitable for estimating cash resale value.

Calculator Value vs Insurance Appraisal

Insurance appraisals generally estimate what it could cost to replace an item through an appropriate retail market.

That amount may include the diamond, setting, craftsmanship, taxes and the cost of sourcing a comparable piece. It is not normally the amount available through an immediate sale.

Entering an insurance value into a resale calculator does not make the appraisal a market offer. The two valuations use different assumptions.

Our guide to diamond resale value versus insurance appraisal explains the distinction.

Calculator Value vs Final Purchase Offer

A calculator estimates value from data. A purchase offer states what a specific buyer is prepared to pay under stated conditions.

The offer may depend on physical verification, payment terms, shipping, insurance, report matching and current purchasing criteria.

A calculator cannot commit funds, take ownership or guarantee that the diamond fits a buyer’s inventory.

Before accepting, determine whether the displayed amount is an estimate, conditional offer or confirmed net payment.

Why Accurate Inputs Matter

A calculator can only work with the information supplied.

If a natural diamond is mistakenly entered as laboratory-grown—or the reverse—the resulting estimate may be completely unsuitable. Guessing that a stone is one carat when it actually weighs 0.70 carats can create another large error.

Colour and clarity should not be estimated from casual photographs. Lighting, camera processing, magnification and the setting can change how a diamond appears.

Whenever possible, enter the characteristics from a verifiable grading report rather than from memory, a receipt or an old insurance appraisal.

Natural vs Laboratory-Grown Origin

Origin is one of the most important calculator inputs.

Natural and laboratory-grown diamonds can have comparable beauty and physical properties, but they operate in separate resale markets with different supply and pricing conditions.

A calculator that does not ask whether the diamond is natural or laboratory-grown should be treated cautiously.

If origin is unknown, the output should be a very broad preliminary indication rather than a confident estimate. Specialised testing may be necessary before value can be calculated responsibly.

Why Carat Weight Is Easy to Enter Incorrectly

Carat measures weight rather than visible size. One metric carat equals 0.20 grams.

A loose diamond can be weighed precisely. A mounted stone cannot normally be weighed separately without professional removal, so any carat figure may be an estimate unless supported by a matching laboratory report.

People also confuse total carat weight with centre-stone weight. A ring described as “one carat total weight” may contain a smaller centre stone surrounded by several additional diamonds.

Entering the total weight as though it belonged to one diamond can produce a greatly overstated result.

Why Colour and Clarity Estimates Cause Errors

Colour and clarity are professionally graded under controlled conditions.

A mounted diamond can reflect colour from the metal. Dirt and lighting can make it appear warmer or duller. Photographs can alter white balance and contrast.

Clarity is assessed under magnification. A visible dark inclusion and a pale inclusion close to the edge may produce different market reactions even when the stones share a grade.

A calculator normally sees only the selected grade. It cannot determine whether an SI1 diamond is eye-clean or contains a prominent inclusion beneath the table.

Why Cut Quality Matters

Cut affects brightness, fire, scintillation, apparent size and buyer demand.

A calculator that asks only for carat, colour and clarity may treat two very different diamonds as equivalent. One could have Excellent cut and balanced proportions, while the other appears dark or small for its weight.

For qualifying round brilliant diamonds, a recognised report may provide an overall cut grade. The calculator should still consider measurements, polish and symmetry where possible.

Fancy shapes require more individual interpretation because an overall standard GIA cut grade is not provided for oval, pear, cushion, emerald and other non-round shapes.

Why Shape Changes Calculator Accuracy

Round brilliant diamonds are relatively standardised and widely compared in the market. This can make report-based calculation more consistent.

Fancy shapes vary considerably. Two one-carat ovals can share the same colour and clarity while having different outlines, ratios, bow-ties and face-up dimensions.

Emerald cuts may differ in windowing and contrast. Cushions can have different facet patterns, while pears and marquises require balanced symmetry and intact points.

A calculator selecting “oval” or “cushion” cannot fully evaluate these visual differences.

Why Proportions and Face-Up Size Matter

Two diamonds with the same carat weight can look different in size.

A deep diamond may carry hidden weight below the girdle and appear smaller face-up. A shallow diamond may appear wider but suffer from weak light performance.

Round-diamond calculators may use table, depth, crown and pavilion information when available. Basic tools often ignore these fields.

For fancy shapes, length, width, depth, ratio and actual outline can have a material effect on demand.

Why Fluorescence Can Change the Result

Fluorescence does not create a standard premium or deduction.

Its effect depends on intensity, colour, the diamond’s body colour, transparency and market preferences. Medium blue fluorescence may have little negative effect and can complement the appearance of some warmer diamonds.

Strong or Very Strong fluorescence may narrow demand in certain high-colour categories, particularly if transparency is affected.

A calculator that automatically deducts the same percentage for every fluorescent diamond may oversimplify the market.

Why Grading Laboratory Matters

The laboratory influences how buyers interpret the documented characteristics.

A GIA, IGI or HRD Antwerp report can provide useful information, but the buyer still verifies the report and physical diamond. Report types, terminology and market familiarity differ.

Some calculators do not ask which laboratory issued the grades. They may assume that every report using identical letters is interpreted in exactly the same way.

For a valuable stone, this can make the estimate less dependable.

Read our GIA vs IGI vs HRD report comparison for additional context.

Why Report Verification Matters

A calculator may produce a detailed estimate from a report number without proving that the stone matches the record.

A genuine report can be presented with the wrong diamond. The stone may also have been chipped, repolished or recut after grading.

The report number should be checked through the laboratory’s official database. The physical diamond should then be matched through shape, measurements, inscription and identifying characteristics.

Our guide explains how to read and verify a diamond grading report.

Condition Is a Major Calculator Limitation

Most calculators assume the diamond remains in normal, undamaged condition.

A chip, cavity, abrasion or damaged point can affect appearance, durability and the cost of making the stone marketable again. The buyer may need to estimate recutting or repolishing.

Corrective work can reduce carat weight. If a 1.01-carat diamond falls below one carat after repair, the lost weight category may have a meaningful financial effect.

Photographs can reveal obvious damage, but minor chips and girdle issues may require magnification.

Treatments Are Difficult to Calculate Automatically

Colour and clarity treatments can affect marketability.

Fracture filling, laser drilling, HPHT processing, irradiation and coating do not have one universal value effect. The type, stability, documentation and disclosure all matter.

A calculator that does not ask about treatments may assume the stone is untreated.

If treatment information appears in the report comments, it must be included in the valuation request.

Transparency and Haziness

Two diamonds with identical report grades can differ in transparency.

Concentrated clouds, internal graining, surface contamination or other characteristics may create a hazy or milky appearance. The report comments can provide clues, but the physical stone remains important.

An automatic calculator rarely evaluates how transparent the diamond looks in several lighting environments.

A clear, lively stone may attract more demand than a hazy diamond with the same headline 4Cs.

Calculators Cannot Fully Assess Inclusions

Clarity grade is a category rather than a complete visual description.

An SI1 diamond with a pale inclusion near the edge can appeal differently from an SI1 containing a dark crystal beneath the table.

Inclusion position may also affect durability. A surface-reaching feature near a vulnerable point requires different consideration from a small internal crystal.

An expert can review the clarity plot and images, but physical magnification provides the strongest assessment.

Calculators Struggle With Antique Diamonds

Old European, old mine, rose and other antique cuts were produced according to different proportions and aesthetic preferences.

A calculator designed for modern diamonds may interpret their depth, culet, symmetry or outline as weaknesses without recognising historical character.

The original setting, age, maker and provenance may also contribute value.

An antique diamond should not be recut or removed from its jewellery simply to fit a modern calculator’s input fields.

Branded Jewellery Requires Separate Assessment

A calculator often values the centre diamond and metal while ignoring the jewellery’s maker.

A signed ring from a recognised jewellery house may carry value through its design, documentation, serial number, craftsmanship and condition.

Removing the centre stone can reduce the value of the complete piece. The same problem can occur with fine antique jewellery.

Submit branded jewellery intact and include the box, receipt, service record and other documents where available.

Small Diamonds and Total Carat Weight

Calculators designed for a single centre stone may not work for pavé, halo, tennis bracelets or multi-stone jewellery.

Several small diamonds do not necessarily equal the value of one diamond with the same combined carat weight. Individual stone size, matching, setting condition and removal costs matter.

A five-carat tennis bracelet therefore cannot be valued by entering “five carats” into a loose centre-diamond calculator.

The complete jewellery item requires a different assessment method.

Regional Market Differences

A calculator may use data from the United States, Europe or another market without explaining the source.

Currency, taxes, buyer demand, common grading reports and popular shapes can differ by region.

A result displayed in euros may simply be converted from another currency rather than calculated using European market evidence.

The tool should state its currency, valuation date and market basis. Otherwise, the output may create false precision.

How Market Data Becomes Outdated

Diamond markets change. Supply, demand and buyer inventory can move even when the physical stone remains unchanged.

A calculator using old retail listings or historical price tables may not reflect the current resale market.

Laboratory-grown pricing can be especially sensitive to changes in production and supply. Natural-diamond demand also varies across size and quality categories.

An evergreen calculator needs regularly reviewed data. A permanent static chart cannot remain accurate indefinitely.

Asking Price vs Completed Transaction Data

Some tools use advertised prices rather than actual transactions.

An online listing shows what the seller hopes to receive. It does not confirm that a buyer paid that amount.

Completed transactions can provide stronger evidence, but they may still involve different regions, services, warranties or payment terms.

A good valuation considers comparable diamonds and the reality of what buyers are currently prepared to pay.

Why Calculators Often Show a Wide Range

A wide range is not always a weakness. It may honestly reflect uncertainty.

If origin, laboratory, condition or inclusion appearance is unknown, a narrow estimate would create misleading confidence.

The range should become more precise as verified information is added. A physical assessment can then resolve factors an algorithm cannot see.

A calculator returning one exact number from minimal information may be less reliable than a tool that explains its uncertainty.

Why Calculator Results Differ From One Website to Another

Different tools may estimate different types of value.

One may use new retail prices, another may estimate insurance replacement and a third may calculate an immediate buyer offer. Their data sources, update schedules and assumptions can also differ.

Some tools incorporate the grading laboratory and fluorescence, while others use only carat, colour and clarity.

Before comparing the numbers, confirm that the calculators are answering the same question.

What Makes a Diamond Calculator More Reliable?

A more useful calculator first identifies whether the diamond is natural or laboratory-grown and loose or mounted.

It should request the grading laboratory, report number, carat, shape, colour, clarity and cut. Additional information such as measurements, polish, symmetry, fluorescence, treatments and condition can improve the estimate.

The tool should define whether the output is retail, replacement, resale or purchase-offer value. It should also state the market, currency and date of its pricing information.

Finally, it should explain that the result is preliminary and subject to report and physical verification.

Warning Signs of a Misleading Calculator

Be cautious when a calculator promises a guaranteed selling price without examining the diamond.

A tool asking only for carat weight cannot responsibly distinguish natural from laboratory-grown origin, colour, clarity or condition.

An exact figure with no range, valuation purpose, data date or explanation may create an impression of accuracy that the underlying information does not support.

Pressure to ship immediately, pay an undisclosed fee or accept an expiring offer should also be treated cautiously.

Online Calculator vs Expert Online Valuation

An automated calculator applies rules to entered data. An expert-reviewed online valuation allows a specialist to examine the report, photographs and context.

The specialist may notice that the report is for a laboratory-grown diamond, the shape carries excessive depth or the item appears branded. These observations can materially change the preliminary result.

The online expert still cannot confirm every characteristic from photographs. Physical inspection may be necessary before the amount becomes final.

Read what happens after requesting an online diamond valuation for the complete process.

Can Artificial Intelligence Value a Diamond?

AI can organise report information, explain the 4Cs and compare documented characteristics. It may also help identify missing information.

It cannot confirm that the report belongs to the physical stone or reliably detect every inclusion, treatment, chip or transparency concern from ordinary photographs.

An AI response also needs current, relevant market data and a clearly defined valuation purpose. Without those elements, a confident figure may still be unsuitable.

AI is most useful as part of a structured preliminary review—not as a substitute for gemological verification and a real purchase offer.

Illustrative Example: Verified One-Carat Round Diamond

Imagine a fictional natural 1.00-carat round diamond with a verifiable report stating G colour, VS2 clarity and Excellent cut.

A detailed calculator can use those grades to create a useful preliminary range. Its accuracy improves if it also includes the laboratory, measurements, fluorescence, polish and symmetry.

The final amount may still change if inspection reveals damage, a prominent inclusion, haziness or a report mismatch.

The calculator is useful because the inputs are verified, but it cannot complete the physical checks.

Illustrative Example: A Ring With Guessed Details

Suppose someone owns a ring described by a relative as containing “about a one-carat diamond.”

The seller selects one carat, natural origin, G colour and VS clarity without documentation. The calculator produces a high estimate.

Inspection later finds that the centre stone weighs significantly less, has lower grades or is laboratory-grown. The estimate fails because the inputs were assumptions rather than verified facts.

Selecting “unknown” and requesting an expert review would have produced a more responsible result.

Illustrative Example: Two Ovals With the Same Grades

Consider two fictional natural 1.50-carat ovals with identical colour and clarity grades.

The first has balanced proportions, attractive face-up dimensions and a mild bow-tie. The second is deep, looks smaller and displays a strong dark bow-tie.

A basic calculator may value them similarly. A buyer examining the physical stones may produce different offers because their marketability is not the same.

Illustrative Example: Insurance Value Entered as Resale Value

Imagine a ring with an insurance appraisal of €12,000.

The owner enters that amount into a website expecting a similar resale result. The calculator reinforces the expectation because it uses retail replacement data.

A buyer’s offer is lower because it reflects the verified diamond and current secondary market rather than the cost of obtaining a replacement from a retailer.

Neither figure is automatically false. They answer different valuation questions.

Illustrative Example: Antique Branded Ring

Suppose an inherited ring contains an old-cut diamond and a recognised maker’s signature.

A loose-diamond calculator may assign a modest amount because the proportions do not resemble a modern brilliant. It may also ignore the maker and original setting.

A specialist may find that the complete ring has additional period or collector appeal.

This is why distinctive jewellery should be assessed intact.

How to Use a Diamond Calculator Responsibly

Begin by identifying what the calculator claims to estimate. Do not compare a retail-price result with a resale offer.

Use verified grading-report information wherever possible. If you do not know a field, select “unknown” rather than choosing the grade that looks closest in a photograph.

Treat the output as a range. Record the currency, date and assumptions so you can compare it with an expert-reviewed valuation.

Do not ship or transfer a diamond solely because an automated result looks attractive. Confirm the buyer, inspection process, insurance, return terms and final payment conditions first.

What to Submit for a Better Online Valuation

Provide the complete grading report, including measurements, comments and report number. Add clear photographs of the full item, side profile and underside.

Mention whether the diamond is natural, laboratory-grown or unknown. Disclose damage, treatments, recutting, repairs and brand information.

If the diamond is mounted, leave it in its setting. A professional can determine whether removal is necessary after the initial review.

The more reliable the information, the narrower and more useful the preliminary estimate can become.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are online diamond calculators accurate?

They can provide a useful preliminary range when supplied with verified information. They cannot normally confirm a final selling price.

How close is a calculator to the final diamond offer?

It varies. Accuracy depends on the inputs, pricing data, diamond type, condition and whether the tool estimates resale value.

Can a calculator tell me exactly what my diamond is worth?

No. It can estimate from supplied information, but a final value normally requires report and physical verification.

Why do calculators give different values?

They may use different data, markets and valuation purposes. One could estimate retail while another estimates resale.

Is a free diamond calculator trustworthy?

It can be useful, but free access does not prove accuracy. Review its inputs, assumptions, data date and valuation definition.

Is a paid calculator more accurate?

Not necessarily. Accuracy depends on methodology and information quality rather than price alone.

What information does a diamond calculator need?

Useful inputs include origin, carat, shape, colour, clarity, cut, laboratory, measurements, fluorescence, finish and condition.

Can carat weight alone calculate diamond value?

No. Diamonds of the same weight can differ substantially in quality, origin and demand.

Can I estimate carat from a photograph?

Not reliably. Scale, perspective, shape and setting can distort apparent size.

Can I calculate a mounted diamond’s exact weight?

Not normally without removal or a matching report. Measurements may support an estimate.

Is total carat weight the same as centre-stone weight?

No. Total carat weight includes all diamonds in the item.

Can a calculator grade diamond colour from a photo?

Not reliably. Lighting, metal reflections, cameras and screens distort colour.

Can a calculator grade clarity from a photo?

Ordinary photographs cannot reliably establish clarity. Magnification and controlled examination are required.

Can an AI photograph tool grade a diamond?

It may identify visible features, but it cannot replace laboratory grading or physical inspection.

Can ChatGPT calculate diamond resale value?

It can explain the factors and organise report data, but it cannot confirm a final market value without verified characteristics and relevant current market evidence.

Does the calculator need a grading report?

Not always, but verified report data can substantially improve the estimate.

Can I use a calculator without a certificate?

Yes, but the range should remain broad until origin and quality are confirmed.

Does a GIA report make the calculator more accurate?

A verifiable report provides reliable quality inputs, but the stone must still match it and remain in the documented condition.

Can I enter an IGI or HRD report?

A detailed calculator may accept those reports. The laboratory and exact report type should be identified.

Does the grading laboratory affect calculator results?

It can. Buyers may interpret report types and market recognition differently.

Can a calculator verify my report number?

Some tools connect with report data, but you should independently verify the report through the laboratory’s official website.

Does a valid report guarantee an accurate estimate?

No. The report could be paired with the wrong diamond, or the stone could have been damaged since grading.

Do calculators account for chips?

Many do not. Damage generally requires physical examination.

Do calculators account for treatments?

Only if they request and correctly interpret the treatment information.

Do calculators detect lab-grown diamonds?

A calculator cannot test origin. It depends on the user or grading report to provide that information.

What happens if I enter a lab-grown diamond as natural?

The estimate may be seriously inaccurate because the two origins have separate resale markets.

Do calculators consider fluorescence?

Some do. Its actual effect is too individual for a simple universal adjustment.

Do calculators consider polish and symmetry?

Detailed tools may include them, while basic calculators often ignore them.

Do calculators consider diamond shape?

Most should. Shape affects demand, proportions and comparable pricing.

Are round-diamond calculator results more accurate?

They may be more consistent because round brilliants are more standardised. Physical condition and market data still matter.

Why are fancy shapes harder to calculate?

Outline, ratio, bow-tie, windowing and face-up appearance vary even within identical report grades.

Can a calculator assess an oval bow-tie?

Not from report fields alone. Photographs, video and physical viewing are usually required.

Can a calculator assess an emerald-cut window?

Not reliably from the 4Cs alone. Proportions and physical appearance must be reviewed.

Does a calculator consider visible inclusions?

It may use the clarity grade, but it cannot always determine whether an inclusion is dark, central or eye-visible.

Can two diamonds with the same 4Cs have different values?

Yes. Shape, proportions, fluorescence, inclusion appearance, transparency, laboratory and condition may differ.

Do calculators account for milky or hazy diamonds?

Most automated tools cannot assess transparency reliably.

Do calculators value antique diamonds correctly?

General modern-diamond calculators may overlook historical cut and collector appeal.

Can a calculator value a branded ring?

A loose-diamond calculator may ignore maker, design, documentation and complete-piece demand.

Can I use a diamond calculator for a tennis bracelet?

A single-stone calculator is not appropriate for multi-stone jewellery.

Can I value earrings by entering their combined carat weight?

Not accurately. Matching, individual weights, grades, condition and setting matter.

Can a calculator value a fancy-colour diamond?

A specialised tool may provide an initial indication, but natural colour origin and distribution require expert assessment.

Is a Z-colour diamond the same as Fancy Yellow in a calculator?

No. D-to-Z and fancy-colour diamonds use different grading and valuation systems.

Do calculators use current diamond prices?

Some do, while others use old or static data. Look for the valuation date and methodology.

How quickly do diamond prices change?

Market conditions can change over time and affect different categories differently. Estimates should be dated.

Are online asking prices reliable calculator data?

They show what sellers request, not necessarily what buyers actually pay.

Why does my calculator estimate exceed buyer offers?

The calculator may use retail or replacement pricing, ignore costs or assume ideal condition.

Does a lower offer mean the calculator or buyer is dishonest?

Not automatically. First determine whether they use different value definitions and verified characteristics.

Is an online calculator the same as an appraisal?

No. An automated estimate is not necessarily a formal professional appraisal.

Can I use a calculator result for insurance?

Insurers may require a purpose-specific professional appraisal. Confirm local requirements before relying on an automated result.

Can I use a calculator result for probate or tax?

Formal legal or tax purposes may require a qualified, purpose-specific valuation. Requirements differ by country.

Can I use a calculator during divorce proceedings?

An automated result may be insufficient for a disputed legal valuation. Obtain appropriate local professional advice.

Does an insurance appraisal show resale value?

Usually not. It generally concerns replacement rather than cash resale.

What is an expert-reviewed online valuation?

A specialist reviews the report, photographs and information rather than relying solely on an automatic formula.

Is an expert online valuation final?

It is normally preliminary until the physical item and documentation are verified.

Why is physical inspection necessary?

It confirms identity, origin, quality, condition, treatments, transparency and report matching.

Should I remove my diamond before using a calculator?

No. Use available report information or select mounted or unknown. Do not remove the stone yourself.

Should I clean the diamond first?

Gentle safe cleaning may improve photographs, but it is unnecessary for the calculation. Avoid risky methods.

Can a calculator tell whether my diamond needs recutting?

No. A cutter or specialist must evaluate the likely improvement, weight loss and risk.

Should I recut the diamond to match a better calculator grade?

No. Obtain a professional economic assessment before altering the stone.

Is an exact calculator number more reliable than a range?

Not necessarily. A reasonable range often reflects uncertainty more honestly.

How wide should a preliminary range be?

There is no standard width. It depends on how much verified information is available.

What should a trustworthy calculator disclose?

It should define the valuation type, inputs, currency, market, data date and need for verification.

What are the biggest calculator warning signs?

Guaranteed prices, minimal inputs, undisclosed assumptions, pressure tactics and no explanation of resale versus retail are significant concerns.

Should I provide my report number?

A specialist may need it for verification. Use a secure form and avoid publicly posting unrelated personal details.

Can a calculator sell my personal information?

Data practices depend on the website. Review its privacy policy before submitting contact or report information.

Do I have to accept an offer after using a calculator?

No. A calculator or free valuation should not create an obligation to sell unless you explicitly agree to different terms.

Can the calculator result decrease after inspection?

Yes. A preliminary estimate may change if the grades, origin, condition or report match cannot be confirmed.

Can the final offer increase after inspection?

Potentially. Inspection may confirm stronger characteristics or additional jewellery value not captured online.

How do I compare calculator results?

Make sure every result estimates the same type of value, currency, date and diamond characteristics.

How do I compare a calculator with a buyer offer?

Compare the calculator’s assumptions with the buyer’s written net amount, fees, conditions and payment terms.

Can Sothis review my calculator estimate?

Sothis can review the underlying diamond information and explain whether the automated estimate reflects a realistic current resale basis.

Move From an Automated Estimate to a Verified Offer

A diamond calculator can help you create an initial valuation profile, particularly when you have a verifiable grading report.

It cannot confirm the physical diamond’s identity, origin, inclusion appearance, transparency, condition or complete marketability. These factors can materially change what a buyer is prepared to pay.

Submit the complete report, clear photographs and any information about treatments, damage, brand or repairs for an expert-reviewed initial valuation. Following physical verification, Sothis Diamonds can provide a market-based offer that you remain free to accept or decline.

Request a free, no-obligation diamond valuation
